---
title: "Comparing cudaGlmnet with glmnet"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Comparing cudaGlmnet with glmnet}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaGlmnet)
HAS_GLMNET <- requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)
if (!HAS_GLMNET) {
  message("glmnet is not installed: the comparison chunks are shown ",
          "but not run.")
}
```

`cudaGlmnet` and `glmnet` fit the same Gaussian lasso problem

`F(beta) = 1/(2n) ||y - a0 - X beta||^2 + lambda ||beta||_1`

Both fit an unpenalised intercept, scale the columns to unit population
(`1/n`) variance, and return coefficients on the original scale. `glmnet`
solves the objective by coordinate descent; `cuda_glmnet()` uses GPU FISTA
through `rcupp`. Same convex problem, different algorithm, so the two agree
to solver tolerance rather than bit-for-bit. This vignette checks that on
one small example.

`glmnet` is in `Suggests`. When it is not installed the comparison chunks
below are shown but not evaluated, so the vignette still renders.

## One lasso fit, two packages

```{r data}
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(60 * 5), 60, 5)
y <- drop(X %*% c(2, -1, 0, 0, 0)) + rnorm(60, sd = 0.5)
lambda <- 0.05
```

Both calls use their defaults (`standardize = TRUE`, `intercept = TRUE`)
and the same penalty `lambda`:

```{r fits, eval = HAS_GLMNET}
g  <- glmnet::glmnet(X, y, lambda = lambda)
cg <- cuda_glmnet(X, y, lambda = lambda)
```

`coef()` returns an intercept row plus one row per variable in both
packages:

```{r coefs, eval = HAS_GLMNET}
b_glmnet <- as.matrix(stats::coef(g, s = lambda))
b_cuda   <- coef(cg, s = lambda)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    term      = rownames(b_cuda),
    glmnet    = drop(b_glmnet),
    cudaGlmnet = drop(b_cuda)
  ),
  digits = 6,
  caption = "Gaussian lasso coefficients at lambda = 0.05."
)
```

The largest coefficient difference is at the solver tolerance, not at the
scale of the estimates:

```{r difference, eval = HAS_GLMNET}
max_diff <- max(abs(b_glmnet - b_cuda))
cat(sprintf("max |glmnet - cudaGlmnet| = %.3e\n", max_diff))
stopifnot(max_diff < 1e-3)
```

Predictions agree for the same reason:

```{r predictions, eval = HAS_GLMNET}
p_glmnet <- drop(as.matrix(stats::predict(g, X[1:5, ], s = lambda)))
p_cuda   <- drop(predict(cg, X[1:5, ], s = lambda))
cat(sprintf("max |prediction difference| = %.3e\n",
            max(abs(p_glmnet - p_cuda))))
```

## A short lambda path

`cuda_glmnet()` also accepts the glmnet-style `s` selection, so a whole
path can be compared at shared penalty values without refitting:

```{r path, eval = HAS_GLMNET}
grid <- c(0.20, 0.10, 0.05)
g_path  <- glmnet::glmnet(X, y, lambda = grid)
cg_path <- cuda_glmnet(X, y, lambda = grid)

B_glmnet <- as.matrix(stats::coef(g_path, s = grid))
B_cuda   <- coef(cg_path, s = grid)
cat(sprintf("lambda path             : %s\n",
            paste(sprintf("%.3f", grid), collapse = ", ")))
cat(sprintf("max |coef difference|   : %.3e\n",
            max(abs(B_glmnet - B_cuda))))
cat(sprintf("non-zero counts agree   : %s\n",
            identical(as.integer(colSums(abs(B_glmnet[-1L, ]) > 1e-8)),
                      as.integer(colSums(abs(B_cuda[-1L, ]) > 1e-8)))))
```

## Why the numbers are not bit-identical

Coordinate descent and FISTA approach the same optimum from different
directions, and each stops at its own convergence threshold (`glmnet`'s
`thresh` and `cuda_glmnet()`'s `tol`). Tightening our solver's tolerance
shrinks the gap by roughly two orders of magnitude:

```{r tighter, eval = HAS_GLMNET}
cg_tight  <- cuda_glmnet(X, y, lambda = lambda, tol = 1e-10)
b_tight   <- coef(cg_tight, s = lambda)
d_default <- max_diff
d_tight   <- max(abs(b_glmnet - b_tight))
cat(sprintf("default tol (1e-6) : %.3e\n", d_default))
cat(sprintf("tol = 1e-10        : %.3e\n", d_tight))
```

## Takeaway

For the Gaussian family, a `cuda_glmnet()` fit is the same lasso solution
as `glmnet::glmnet()`: same intercept, same standardisation, same
coefficients and same predictions at a shared `lambda`. The residual
difference is solver tolerance, not a different model.
